Kārtavīryārjuna
------------------------------------------
Arjuna, the son of the king Kṛtavīrya of चन्द्रवṁश (lunar dynasty) was better known as ‘Kārtavīryārjuna’. He was the king of माहिष्मती in the विन्ध्य mountain range. A devotee of दत्तात्रेय (See DATTĀTREYA.) he had secured the boon of getting one thousand arms during any war he would fight.
He had once defeated the mighty रावण in a battle and had taken him captive. रावण’s ड़थेर्, the sage पुलस्त्य, had to intervene to get him released.
During hunting, one day, he happened to enter the hermitage of the sage जमदग्नि and was sumptuously fed by him. The cow Kapilā endowed with divine powers had helped him to entertain the guests. When कार्तवीर्यार्जुन asked for it to be gifted to him, the sage refused. Offended by this refusal, the king killed the sage. On hearing this, however, परशुराम, जमदग्नि’s son, went to Māhiṣmati, killed the king, decimated his army and destroyed his city.

karmamārga
(‘the path of कर्म or action’)
------------------------------------------
From the most ancient times, the Vedic religion has kept before man, two paths—karmamārga (the path of action) and ज्ञानमार्ग (the path of knowledge). Since the former advocates activism, whereas the latter upholds withdrawal from actions except those needed for main-taining the body for sādhanā or spiritual practice, the two are also called, respectively, pravṛtti-mārga and निवृत्ति-mārga.
In the कर्ममार्ग, a person entitled for it, has to avoid निषिद्धकर्म (prohi-bited or sinful actions), perform नित्य and naimittika karmas (obligatory daily actions and occasional ones) without selfish motives, as a duty and in a spirit of worship of God. This purifies him gradually, enabling him to go to higher worlds like पितृलोक or the world of manes through the Dhūmādimārga, the path of smoke.
Performance of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् like the अग्निहोत्र and the दर्शपूर्णमास as also several others including those motivated by unfulfilled desires, are also included in this कर्ममार्ग.
See also KARMAYOGA.

Karṇa
------------------------------------------
If fate, the invincible power, can ever be accused of messing up things, it is in the life of कर्ण. Born to a would-be queen by the grace of no less a deity than the Sun-god himself, he was condemned to live and die in the shadow of an irredeemable villain.
He was the first offspring of कुन्ती, the elder queen of the king पाण्डु. She begot him before her मर्रिअगे when she experimented with the powerful मन्त्र taught to her by the sage दुर्वासस्, by invoking सूर्य or the Sun-god. Afraid of calumny, she abandoned the baby-son in the stream of a river. For Adhiratha and राधा, a couple of the charioteer caste, who retrieved the baby it was a god-send since they were childless. They christened him as Vasuṣeṇa. However he was more well-known as कर्ण, Rādheya (son of राधा), Ādhirathi (son of Adhiratha) and Sūtaputra (son of a सूत or a person of the charioteer caste) being the other names.
After becoming an adept in the use of various weapons, he approached the warrior-sage परशुराम for higher training in the use of arms. This he did in the guise of a ब्राह्मण since the sage was a sworn enemy of the kṣattriyas and would never accept them as disciples. However almost at the end of the period of training, the truth was out. The sage cursed him for having cheated him by telling a lie as a result of which कर्ण would not be able to remember the appropriate formulae connected with the divine weapons, during the most critical moments in a war.
When the Pāṇḍavas were being tested for their prowess and proficiency in the use of arms at the close of their training period, कर्ण appeared on the scene throwing a challenge that he could do better than them. However, since he belonged to a caste lower than that of the kṣattriyas, he was not allowed to compete with them. Consequently he was dejected. दुर्योधन, the eldest of the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍava-baiter at that, seized this opportunity, accepted him as a friend on equal terms and even crowned him as the king of Aṅgadeśa, the country called ‘Aṅga’.
This disgrace, as also the humiliation he had to suffer at द्रौपदी’s स्वयṁवर (ceremony of a maiden choosing her husband) made him an inveterate enemy of the Pāṇḍavas, especially of अर्जुन.
Karṇa now became the right-hand man of दुर्योधन and antagonised the Pāṇḍavas at every opportunity he could seize. His part in the ugly and indecent act of दुश्शासन trying to disrobe द्रौपदी was not insignificant.
At the beginning of the कुरुक्षेत्र war, कृष्ण tried to win him over to the side of the Pāṇḍavas by disclosing his real identity as the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas. However, कर्ण’s loyalty to दुर्योधन prevented him from being tempted to change sides.
A tiff with भीष्म, the first commander-in-chief of the Kaurava army, forced कर्ण to withdraw from the कुरुक्षेत्र war as long as he lived and led the army. It was only after the withdrawal of भीष्म from the war-front, that कर्ण joined the fray.
Though he fought valiantly, first as a great warrior and later as the commander-in-chief, he was ultimately killed by अर्जुन in the single combat with him.

karaṇḍa-mukuṭa
(‘crown resembling a basket’)
------------------------------------------
Images of Hindu gods, goddesses and lesser divinities have, almost always, a मुकुट or a crown on their heads. One of the several varieties of such crowns is the करण्ड-मुकुट. ‘Karaṇḍa’ means a basket, usually made of bamboo strips. Hence a करण्ड-मुकुट is a crown that resembles a basket of bamboo strips.
मुकुट.jpg" src="http://eoh.rkmathbangalore.org/public/images/thumbs/kara%E1%B9%87%E1%B8%8Da-muku%E1%B9%ADa.jpg" alt="karaṇḍa-मुकुट">Usually female deities and some minor gods like गणपति or yakṣas are provided with karaṇḍa-mukuṭas.
This type of crown has three round basket-like shapes in three, five or seven tiers. The lower one is studded with jewels and has a golden band. The topmost one is surmounted by a śikhāmaṇi or crest-jewel.

karṇarandhra-dhauti
(‘cleaning of the ear-passages’)
------------------------------------------
Cleansing the various parts of the body is an important aspect of हठयोग. Such processes are called ‘dhauti’. कर्णरन्ध्र-धौति is the 3rd and the 4th part of दन्तधौति. It consists of cleaning the two holes or passages of the ears, using the index or the ring fingers. By practising it daily, some mystical sounds are supposed to be heard, according to the Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā (1.33).
See also DANTADHAUTI and DHAUTI.

kāraṇaśarīra
(‘causal body’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Vedānta philosophy as depicted in the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahma-sūtras and allied scriptures, every जीव or individual सोउल् has three śarīras or bodies: sthūla (gross), sūkṣma (subtle) and कारण (causal).
The कारणशरीर or causal body is nothing but अज्ञान or इग्नोरन्चे which is the root-cause of embodiment and hence, transmigration.
See also JĪVA.

Karmakāṇḍa
(‘branch [of the Veda dealing with] कर्म or rituals’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu tradition generally divides the वेदस् into two broad groups: कर्मकाण्ड and ज्ञानकाण्ड.
The ज्ञानकाण्ड comprises the उपनिषद्स्.
The कर्मकाण्ड deals with the various Vedic rituals including the yāgas or sacrifices. The ब्राह्मणस् are the main content of the कर्मकाण्ड. The mantras in the Saṁhitā section are chanted at the appropriate stages in the performance of the Vedic rites.
Whereas the Vedāntic systems give the कर्मकाण्ड a lower place, the Mīmāṁsā system makes it the chief aspect of the वेदस् assigning to the Vedānta (or the Upaniṣadic section) a subsidiary place.
See also JÑĀNAKĀṆḌA.

karanyāsa
(‘dedication or purification of the hand’)
------------------------------------------
Nyāsa or purification of limbs is an important aspect of many a ritualistic process like पूजा (worship), जप (repetition of divine name) and pārāyaṇa (ceremonial recitation of scriptures or sacred texts). Out of seven such nyāsas, the अङ्गन्यास and the करन्यास are most common.
In the करन्यास, the fingers of both the hands are purified simultaneously to the accompaniment of appropriate mantras. First, the thumbs are rubbed by the tips of the index-fingers from bottom to top with the मन्त्र ‘aṅguṣṭābhyaṁ namaḥ’. Then the thumbs do the rest of the work in a similar manner, to the other four fingers, the mantras being changed according to the fingers touched.
See also AṄGANYĀSA and NYĀSA.

kārya
(‘that which is done’)
------------------------------------------
Widely used, this word has several senses.
As associated with the word ‘kāraṇa’ (cause), it means the effect. For instance, if clay is the कारण, pot is its कार्य or effect.
Some of the other senses in which it is used are: work, conduct, utility, profession and duty.
The word is also used in a more technical sense in अस्त्रोलोग्य् and legal works.
See also KĀRAṆA.

karmamīmāṁsā
(‘enquiry [into the philosophy of] Vedic rituals’)
------------------------------------------
It is the philosophical system that tries to determine the correct meaning of the कर्मकाण्ड part of the वेदस्. It is the same as the Mīmāṁsā philosophy.
See MĪMĀṀSĀDARŚANA for details.

Karmayoga
(‘yoga of कर्म or action’)
------------------------------------------
According to all the six systems of Hindu philosophy, especially the Vedānta, मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from the cycle of transmigration, is the final goal of human life. This can be got by realising God—called आत्मन् or ब्रह्मन् or Īśvara—who is not only transcendent but also immanent in every object of the universe including the human being. This can be done either by ज्ञान (knowledge) or by भक्ति (devotion) through the respective paths known as ज्ञानयोग and भक्तियोग.
However, all the schools of Vedānta concede that निष्कामकर्म (ordained actions performed without the taint of selfish desires) purifies the mind—this is called ‘cittaśuddhi’—making it fit for the paths of either ज्ञान or भक्ति.
If God is in the heart of every human being and if the impurity of मिन्द् is preventing him from getting God-experience, removing that impurity should do the trick. And, निष्कामकर्म pursued till the whole मिन्द् is completely purified, must be able to achieve this and hence God-realisation as well as मोक्ष too! This is the line of argument of those who advocate that कर्मयोग also, like the other yogas, can be an independent path leading to मोक्ष. And, there is enough support in the scriptures for this school also (vide Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad 2, 3 and 4; Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad 2; Bhagavadgītā 3.20; 5.19; 18.46; Viṣṇupurāṇa

and so on).
Man is essentially a social being and cannot live without doing some कर्म or the other. By guiding him in this field of कर्म itself, कर्मयोग shows him the way of spiritual evolution.
Every human being has to work at two levels: the individual or the personal and, the social. The work at the individual level comprises general maintenance of the body and spiritual practices for spiritual evolution. The work at the social level consists of earning one’s livelihood and discharging one’s obligations to the other members of the society, including those of one’s own family.
Our body-मिन्द् complex is the basic instrument for us, to practise any योग. Hence it must be kept in a good condition. In कर्मयोग, since work or activity is all important, this becomes even more vital.
Apart from this, coming to the field of work itself, the spiritual aspirant following the path of कर्मयोग has to implement the following, as a part of his sādhanā:
He has to eschew completely all actions and conduct declared as niṣiddha (sinful and hence prohibited).
He has to renounce all kāmya-कर्म or actions motivated by selfish desires, since they bind him to सṁसार or transmigratory existence.
On the other hand, he should never shirk from doing his ordained duties or kartavyakarmas, however unpleasant they may appear to be. Ordained duties are determined by the scriptures, social conventions and even by what one has voluntarily chosen as a duty (provided it does not transgress the basic principles of धर्म).
Since each is great in his own place, he should never think that his own work (and hence himself) is greater than that of others. Everyone, irrespective of his status in the society or the work that is his ordained duty, is capable of attaining spiritual enlightenment by cultivating the attitude that he is worshipping God through that work.
He should also pay great attention to attaining proficiency in his field of work. Efficient work, done without desires and ambitions, helps one in subjective spiritual evolution. It will also benefit the society greatly. And, if the society is benefited, he too should be benefited.
The epics and the पुराणस् give us the names of quite a few persons who got enlightenment through कर्मयोग. They are: a brāhmin lady (Mahābhārata, Vanaparva 206); धर्मव्याध (op. cit. 209); तुलाधार (Śāntiparva 262); जनक (Bhagavadgītā 3.20).
The saint Puṇḍarīka (10th century A. D.) from Maharashtra may also be taken as an example.
A perfect karmayogi is never attached to anything in this world. He has actually no duties or obligations since he has already attained the final goal of life. However, he is ever active in the world, out of infinite compassion for the suffering human beings and also to set an example to the un-enlightened persons.
Another characteristic of his is that he works like a master and not like a servant or a slave. And, his own work is so perfect that it becomes a model for others to emulate.
See also KARMA.

Kardama
------------------------------------------
A great ṛṣi (sage) considered as one of the nine मिन्द्-born sons of ब्रह्मा, the creator, was an ardent devotee of विष्णु. He pleased विष्णु by his austerities and got the boon of a worthy wife as also the Lord विष्णु himself to be born as his son.
Very soon, मनु, the king of human beings came to his hermitage and offered देवहूति, his daughter, in मर्रिअगे.
Kardama had nine daughters and a son, कपिल, considered as an इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु himself. अनसूया (wife of the sage अत्रि), अरुन्धती (wife of the sage वसिष्ठ) and ख्याति (wife of the sage भृगु) were among these nine daughters.
After completing his duties as a householder, कर्दम advised his wife देवहूति to get spiritual wisdom from her son कपिल, who was none other than Lord विष्णु himself and retired to the forest for austerities.
See also KAPILA.

kāraṇa
(‘that by which something is accomplished’)
------------------------------------------
Indian philosophical systems have devoted some attention to the problem of कारण or cause and कार्य or effect, and their mutual relationship.
Kāraṇa or cause is of various kinds:
Upādānakāraṇa is the material cause, like clay for a pot.
Nimittakāraṇa is the efficient cause like the potter’s wheel and stick as also the potter himself, for the pot.
Samavāyikāraṇa is the inherent cause, as the threads are for the cloth out of which it is woven.
Other examples for samavāyikāraṇa are the existence of a part in a whole, a quality in a qualified object or movement in a moving object.
Asamavāyikāraṇa is the non-inherent cause, like the colour of the threads, which causes the colour of the cloth, after the cloth is woven. Colour is related to the threads directly and indirectly to the cloth.
Mūlakāraṇa is the original cause of the universe, i.e., ब्रह्मन् or God.

karmasaṁnyāsa
(‘renunciation of [all] actions’)
------------------------------------------
As per the smṛtis and धर्मशास्त्रस् (secondary scriptures dealing with personal and social conduct) a गृहस्थ or a householder had to perform a number of rites and rituals. वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् (if he had duly established the Vedic fires), नित्य and naimittika karmas (obligatory and occasional duties), ṣoḍaśa सṁस्कारस् (sacraments) and other duties connected with personal and social life would keep him so busy that he would not get sufficient time and mood for spiritual pursuits. Hence he was advised to hand over the responsibility of running the family to the eldest son and retire to the forest, to lead the life of a वानप्रस्थ (forest-recluse). There, he was to maintain one Vedic fire—the gārhapatya—and perform only the daily अग्निहोत्र apart from the सन्ध्या ritual. Later on, he was advised to send back his wife (if she had accompanied him to the forest) to his eldest son and embrace monastic life which necessarily involved wandering from place to place, depending entirely on God. This type of life, while being conducive to spiritual aspirations, did not allow him to continue the karmas or rituals. (Nor were they necessary now, since he had transcended them.) Hence, he took the vows of कर्मसṁन्यास or renunciation of all rites and actions except those needed for maintaining the body and doing sādhanās.
See also SAṀNYĀSA.

Kārttikeya
(‘son of the presiding goddesses of कृत्तिका’)
------------------------------------------
See SUBRAHMAṆYA.

Kārttikai-dīpam
(‘beacon light [lit on Kārttika pūrṇimā])
------------------------------------------
The कार्त्तिकै-दीपम् festival is observed on the pūrṇimā (full-मोओन्) day of the month of Kārttika (October / November) mostly in Tamil Nadu. Lord शिव is said to have manifested himself in the form of the Aruṇagiri or Aruṇācala hill (at Tiruvaṇṇāmalai, hallowed by the recent memories of रमण महर्षि [A.
-1950]) on this day. A huge beacon is lit on the hill on this day which is witnessed and worshipped by thousands of devotees. It burns for several days.

kartṛtva
(‘doership’, ‘agency of an action’)
------------------------------------------
Though the आत्मन् or the Self, being pure चैतन्य or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is neither the kartā or the agent of an action, nor the bhoktā, the enjoyer of its fruits, the आत्मन् in bondage (called जीव) is.
See BHOKTṚ for details.

karmendriyas
(‘organs of action’)
------------------------------------------
Every human being is endowed with eleven इन्द्रियस् or sense-organs. They are: the five ज्ञानेन्द्रियस्, the five कर्मेन्द्रियस् and the मिन्द्.
The five कर्मेन्द्रियस् or organs of action are: vāk (speech), pāṇi (hands), pāda (feet), pāyu (excretory organ) and upastha (organ of reproduction).
These have been called ‘karmendriyas’ because they are the इन्द्रियस् or sense-organs, responsible for कर्म or action. They are the products of the रजस् aspect of the five तन्मात्रस् (subtle elements) as follows: आकाश (ether, space) gives rise to vāk, वायु (air) to pāṇi, अग्नि (fire) to pāda, āpas (water) to pāyu and पृथ्वी (earth) to upastha.
See also JÑĀNENDRIYAS and TANMĀTRAS.

karṇavedha
(‘piercing the ear-lobes’)
------------------------------------------
Saṁskāras or sacraments (ritual purificatory processes) are common to many religions. One of the minor सṁस्कारस् recommended in the later dharmaśāstra literature is कर्णवेध or piercing the lobes of the ears of a child.
Since both men and women were using ear-ornaments in those days कर्णवेध used to be done both on the female and on the male child.
It used to be performed on the 10th or the 12 or the 16th day from birth. Alternatively, it could be done in the 7th or the 10th month after birth.
The ceremony used to be done by the ड़थेर् of the child with Vedic mantras (vide Ṛgveda 1.89.8) followed by the feeding of the ब्राह्मणस्.
In the modern times, it may be done by a goldsmith with pointed gold wire or even by a doctor.

Kārma-mala
(‘impurities [that arise] due to कर्म’)
------------------------------------------
Śaivism is an important part of हिन्दुइस्म्. The पाशुपत cult is a major aspect of the same.
According to this cult, the जीव or the सोउल् in bondage called ‘paśu’ (or animal) here has three malas or impurities that act as fetters. कार्म-मल is the third of these. It is actually the limitations that arise due to the effect of the past karmas.
Yoga helps the paśujīva to cleanse himself of all the three malas.
See also ĀṆAVAMALA, MĀYĪYAMALA and ŚAIVISM.

karmavipāka
(‘fruition of कर्म’)
------------------------------------------
The theory of कर्म is an extension of the proverb, ‘As you sow, so you reap!’ to the spiritual field. All the actions done by us have a twofold effect: that which is seen here and now; and, their future effect, depending upon whether they are पुण्य (good) or पाप (bad).
The ripening of a part of the accumulated कर्म, to give its result is called ‘karmavipāka’.
See also KARMA.

kārya-कारण-bhāva
(‘cause and effect relationship’)
------------------------------------------
The six systems of Hindu philosophy generally try to establish their doctrines by basing them on the वेदस् and allied scriptures as also लोगिच् and reasoning.
One of the basic topics discussed by these systems is the origin of this world. If this world is here, now, being experienced by our senses and the मिन्द्, it must have had a beginning, an original cause from which it has evolved.
To prove this logically, the theory of cause and effect, and, their mutual relationship has to be stated clearly. This is technically called ‘kārya-कारण-भाव’. Unconditionality and invariability are indispensable for this.
Fire as the cause and smoke as the effect, clay as the cause and a pot as the effect are the examples commonly given.
Arguing backwards, all the schools agree that there must be an original cause or causes for this world. However, as to the number and nature of these causes there are wide differences of opinion.

karma
(‘that which is done’)
------------------------------------------
‘Karma’ is one of the most widely used words in हिन्दुइस्म्. Derived from the root-verb ‘kṛ’ (= to do), its general meaning is anything that is done. In this sense, it means: work; profession; and, duty.
However, more often than not, it is used in a technical sense, as an action that binds one to सṁसार or transmigratory existence. This type of कर्म can be accomplished either by the body or by speech or by the मिन्द्. The respective names for these are: kāyika, वाचिक and mānasa karmas.
Again, this कर्म with the potential to produce its fruits, can be classified as sañcita (accumulated over several lives), prārabdha (begun to bear fruit in this life) and āgāmī (being performed now and in future).
All the darśanas or philosophies that accept this theory of कर्म also concede that:
The effects of karmas done in one life cannot be expected to be exhausted in that life itself. Hence पुनर्जन्म or rebirth has to be accepted.
Jñāna or spiritual wisdom resulting in the realisation of one’s nature as the immortal सोउल्, destroys सञ्चितकर्म completely and makes āgāmī incapable of producing its results even as a burnt seed cannot sprout. However, प्रारब्धकर्म, since it has already started giving its results, has got to be exhausted only through experiencing it.
From another standpoint, कर्म is of two types: निषिद्धकर्म or prohibited or sinful actions that must be avoided; vihita-कर्म or actions ordained by the scriptures as duty, to be performed.
The latter again, is of three types: काम्यकर्म (desire-motivated actions); नित्यकर्म (daily duties); नैमित्तिक-कर्म (occasional duties).
Kāmyakarma is performed to fulfil a desire that cannot, otherwise, be fulfilled by normal human efforts. For instance, the पुत्रकामेष्टि rite said to have been performed by the king दशरथ to get worthy sons, belongs to this category. So also the several vratas (religious vows and rites) like the Satyanārāyaṇa vrata which are common even now.
Ordained daily duties like सन्ध्या-vandana, repetition of the गायत्री मन्त्र and अग्निहोत्र belong to the नित्यकर्म group.
Naimittikakarmas have to be performed due to certain nimittas or the presence of special causes. For instance, during an एच्लिप्से, śrāddhas (obsequial rites) have to be done.
Sometimes, karmas or actions are classified according to their nature, good or bad. Actions done without being tainted by likes and dislikes or selfish motives, (but with noble intent) are called sāttvika (good). If done with these, they become rājasika (mixed). If they are motivated by evil designs, to harm others, they are dubbed as tāmasika (dark or evil).
Occasionally the word ‘karma’ is also used to indicate the सṁस्कारस् or sacraments.

karmāśaya
(‘[the potential result of] कर्म that resides in the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical word that has been used in the योग philosophy (vide Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि 2.12).
When a particular karma—good or bad—is done, its unseen result will ‘lie’ (śete) in the मिन्द् in a subtle form, until it gets a suitable opportunity to be manifested. Such residual कर्म is called ‘karmāśaya’.
This कर्माशय, which may be good or bad, is born out of काम (desire), लोभ (greed), मोह (delusion) or krodha (anger and hatred). For instance, those desiring to attain स्वर्ग or हेअवेन्, perform sacrifices like ज्योतिष्टोम thereby accumulating good कर्माशय. Those who commit sins like cheating or murder, due to greed or anger accumulate bad कर्माशय.
This कर्माशय, if very intense, can produce its effect in this life itself. If not, it is manifested in future births.
The results will, of course, be good or bad according to the merit or demerit of the actions done.
Karmāśaya is sometimes called ‘kārmaśarīra’ also.
See also KARMA.
